title: Rafael and the House
premise: Wren Sandoval, a meticulous pest controller who treats documentation as ritual, takes a routine call to the Aldous house and finds something with fingerprints living in the walls. When every mirror begins reflecting the rooms one second late, Wren realizes the house remembers a theft committed in 1974 — the disappearance of a child, Elise Aldous, whose family buried the truth along with her. As the lag widens from one second to minutes, the house begins pulling Wren into the reflected past, where they must recover what was taken and return it before the lag swallows the present entirely. In the end, Wren returns Elise — her remains, her name, her story — to the house, sacrificing their own reflection to do it, and walks out into a world that no longer shows them back.
about_author: Rafael Ishikawa is a former building inspector who spent a decade cataloguing the structural failures of old houses before turning to horror fiction. They live in a restored 1920s farmhouse and claim, only half-jokingly, to have never once looked in its hallway mirror after dark.

chapters.title: The Call Comes at 4 A.M.
chapters.summary: Wren Sandoval, POV. A pest control job unlike any other: the Aldous house, empty for decades, with a client who insists something is 'moving inside the plaster.' Wren documents everything — photographs, timestamps, measurements. Emotional beat: professional calm masking a low hum of dread; the reader learns documentation is Wren's way of keeping the world fixed and legible.

chapters.title: Something with Fingerprints
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. In the crawlspace, Wren finds smudge trails in the dust — five-fingered, human-sized, but pressed too deep, as if made by something heavier than a body. They photograph the prints; in the photos, the prints face the camera. Emotional beat: the first crack in Wren's certainty that the world can be filed and understood.

chapters.title: The House That Was Left
chapters.summary: Wren, POV, with a phone call from their estranged sister Mara. Research reveals the house's history: the Aldous family, 1974, a daughter named Elise who 'went to live with relatives' and was never mentioned again. Emotional beat: Wren's own unresolved family grief surfaces, braiding their story to the house's.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. The hallway mirror reflects the room a full second behind — Wren raises a hand, and the reflection follows late, then hesitates, then continues a half-motion Wren never made. They film it. The footage shows the reflection looking directly at the lens. Emotional beat: terror sharpened into obsession; Wren cannot stop watching.

chapters.title: The Client Who Isn't There
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. Wren returns to the office to invoice the client — and finds no record of the call, no address, no name. Yet the house's key is still in their pocket, warm. Emotional beat: isolation deepens; the house has chosen Wren, and no one outside will believe or even remember.

chapters.title: What the Neighbors Remember
chapters.summary: Wren, POV, interviewing elderly neighbor Dot Ferris. Dot remembers Elise Aldous: the summer of 1974, the family's hushed panic, the father carrying a heavy tarp to the cellar at 3 a.m. 'They didn't lose her,' Dot says. 'They put her somewhere.' Emotional beat: the horror pivots from supernatural to human — a family's sin, preserved in a house that refuses to forget.

chapters.title: The Cellar Door Was Sealed for a Reason
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. Wren breaks the painted-shut cellar door and finds the room preserved like an exhibit: children's drawings, a small shoe, and a wall of mirrors, every one of them covered in cloth. When Wren uncovers a single mirror, the lag stretches to ten seconds. Emotional beat: transgression and consequence; Wren has touched the wound and the house knows.

chapters.title: The Lag Widens
chapters.summary: Wren, POV, intercut with Mara's voicemails growing frantic. The lag now spans minutes. Wren watches their own reflection live out a parallel evening — eating, sleeping, weeping — and realizes the reflection is not copying them anymore. It is rehearsing something. Emotional beat: the uncanny becomes intimate; Wren is being studied by themselves.

chapters.title: 1974, First Pull
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. Falling asleep in the house, Wren wakes inside the mirror-world: the house in 1974, warm-lit and populated by figures who move like memories — including a girl with a scraped knee who looks at Wren and says, 'You're late too.' Emotional beat: wonder laced with grief; the past is not a place Wren visited but a place that has been waiting.

chapters.title: Elise
chapters.summary: Wren, POV, in the mirror-world. Elise Aldous, eleven years old, is not a ghost but a resident — she has been here fifty years, and she does not know she is dead. She shows Wren the house as it was: the parents' fear, the 'accident' on the cellar stairs, the decision to hide her rather than face the truth. Emotional beat: devastating tenderness; Wren realizes returning Elise means telling her she died.

chapters.title: The Family That Stayed
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. The mirror-world contains the parents too, frozen in the evening of their sin, repeating it nightly — the father carrying the tarp, the mother scrubbing a stain that never lifts. They cannot see Wren, but the father begins to pause, mid-loop, as if hearing something. Emotional beat: pity curdling into horror; guilt has made them permanent residents.

chapters.title: Documentation as Prayer
chapters.summary: Wren, POV, writing in their logbook as the house's influence bleeds into the real world — neighbors report lights, Mara drives out and stands at the gate unable to cross. Wren's notes become a litany, part evidence, part confession. Emotional beat: Wren understands their documentation was never about control; it was a plea to be witnessed, and now the house is witnessing them back.

chapters.title: The Reflection Stops Pretending
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. In the real house, Wren's reflection steps out of the mirror and takes Wren's place at the kitchen table, calmly eating dinner. The real Wren is locked outside their own life — their phone doesn't recognize them, their apartment key doesn't turn. Emotional beat: erasure; the price of the house's attention is becoming replaceable.

chapters.title: Mara at the Gate
chapters.summary: Mara, POV. Mara breaks through whatever held her at the gate and finds Wren — or the thing wearing Wren — who speaks in Wren's voice but uses the wrong hand, laughs at the wrong beats. Mara, who has spent years resenting Wren's distance, recognizes the falseness instantly because she always knew her sibling better than they thought. Emotional beat: estranged love as the story's hidden weapon.

chapters.title: The Terms of Return
chapters.summary: Wren, POV, in the mirror-world. The house speaks through the parents' loops: what was taken must be returned. Elise must be carried out of the mirror-world and given back — to the ground, to her name, to the record. But the mirror keeps what crosses: whoever carries her out leaves their reflection behind, permanently. Emotional beat: the bargain made explicit; survival has a price and Wren must choose it knowingly.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. Wren tells Elise the truth — that she fell, that her parents hid her, that she has been waiting fifty years in a house that loved her too badly to bury her. Elise's reaction is not rage but relief: 'I just wanted someone to say it out loud.' Emotional beat: the thematic heart; the horror was never the ghost, it was the silence.

chapters.title: The Father Wakes
chapters.summary: Wren, POV, in the mirror-world. Breaking the loop alerts the father, who becomes lucid for the first time in fifty years — and desperate, violent, unwilling to let his crime be carried out into the light. The house itself splits its allegiance, walls shifting to block Wren, floorboards opening to guide Elise. Emotional beat: the climax begins; guilt weaponized against truth.

chapters.title: Carrying Her Out
chapters.summary: Wren, POV, with Mara breaking into the real house in parallel. Wren takes Elise's hand and walks her through the collapsing mirror-world toward the cellar mirrors while the father tears the house apart behind them. In the real world, Mara uncovers every mirror and calls Wren's name into them. Emotional beat: relentless forward motion; two siblings converging across a membrane of glass.

chapters.title: The Second of Lag
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. At the threshold, Elise hesitates — crossing means becoming a body, a grave, a finished thing. Wren promises to write her down, to make her real in the record, and Elise steps through. In the real house, the mirrors shatter one by one, and Wren's reflection does not step back out. Emotional beat: the sacrifice paid in full; grief and completion in the same breath.

chapters.title: Burial
chapters.summary: Mara and Wren, alternating POV. They bury Elise's remains — recovered from where the mirror-world left them — under a marker with her full name and dates, and Wren files the true record with the county, ending fifty years of silence. The house goes still. The lag closes. Emotional beat: mourning as repair; documentation finally becomes the prayer it always pretended to be.

chapters.title: The House After
chapters.summary: Wren, POV. Wren returns to the empty Aldous house to close out the job. The mirrors are dark, ordinary, honest. But in the last one, for a single frame, Wren sees the reflection wave goodbye — Elise's small hand, not theirs. Wren waves back and locks the door. Emotional beat: bittersweet release; the haunting ends in gratitude rather than terror.

chapters.title: A Person Without a Reflection
chapters.summary: Wren, POV, epilogue. Months later, Wren lives carefully — avoiding mirrors, letting Mara take the photographs, keeping Elise's file on their desk. In a shop window one evening, Wren's reflection appears for half a second: not their face, but a small girl waving. Wren smiles, and the reflection is gone. Emotional beat: quiet, open-ended grace; the price of survival is paid forever, but memory — kept honestly — is its own kind of company.
